summary: This standards-track memo defines an authentication suboption for the DHCP Relay Agent Information Option from RFC 3046. It carries a keyed hash that lets the DHCP server check that relay-added information is genuine and unmodified, and it provides protection against replay.

plainLanguage.summary: A relay agent carries DHCP messages from a client to a server and adds its own information on the way. This RFC lets the server check that this added information really came from the relay and was not changed or replayed, by putting a secret stamp on the message.

questions: how to authenticate dhcp relay information
what is the dhcp relay authentication suboption
how does dhcp relay agent authentication work
what is the dhcp relay agent information option
how does dhcp replay detection work
subtitle: A keyed hash and a counter that let a DHCP server trust the data a relay agent adds on the way.

tldr.problem: A relay agent adds information to DHCP messages after the client has sent them, and the existing DHCP Authentication option deliberately leaves that added data unprotected, so a server cannot tell whether the relay's data is genuine.
tldr.mechanism: A new Authentication suboption inside the Relay Agent Information option carries a replay counter and an HMAC-SHA1 keyed hash computed over the whole DHCP message.
tldr.outcome: Servers and relays can drop messages that were altered or replayed. The cost is hashing work on every message and shared keys that both ends must be configured with.

today: RFC 4030 is a Proposed Standard from March 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It adds a suboption to the Relay Agent Information option defined in RFC 3046, and it asks IANA for one new suboption code and two new number spaces.

sections.title: Why Relay Data Needs Its Own Protection
sections.content:
DHCP gives IPv4 clients their address and configuration. A relay agent receives a broadcast message from a client and forwards it to a server as a unicast message. In network environments such as DOCSIS data-over-cable and xDSL, the relay agent also adds information to the DHCP message before forwarding it, using the relay-agent information option from RFC 3046.

The kind of information that relays add is often used in the server's decision about which addresses and configuration parameters the client should receive. That makes the added data important, and it makes the trust relationship between the relay agent and the server important too.

The existing DHCP Authentication specification in RFC 3118 covers only communication between the DHCP client and the server. Because relay-agent information is added after the client has sent its message, that authentication explicitly excludes relay-agent data. This RFC defines a new relay-agent suboption, the Authentication suboption, whose format and hash computation are close to those of the DHCP Authentication option.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay agent carries DHCP messages from a client to a server and adds its own information on the way. The server relies on that information when it decides what to give the client, so the server needs to know it really came from the relay and was not changed on the way. This RFC adds a way to check that.

sections.title: The Authentication Suboption
sections.content:
The suboption has a code of 8. The length field counts the algorithm, the replay detection method and all subsequent suboption fields, in octets. The Algorithm field names the algorithm used to generate the authentication information. Four bits are reserved for future use: they should be set to zero and must not be used when the suboption is processed.

The Replay Detection Method (RDM) field names the method used to generate the replay detection data, and the 64-bit Replay Detection field carries a value used to detect replayed messages, interpreted according to that method. The Relay Identifier field is used by relay agents that do not set giaddr. The Authentication Information field carries the data needed for algorithm-specific parameters, as well as the checksum. The checksum is usually a digest of the data in the DHCP packet, computed with the method named by the Algorithm field.
sections.plainLanguage: The new suboption has a code of 8. It names the hashing method, carries a 64-bit counter used to spot replayed messages, holds an identifier for the relay, and carries the hash value itself.

sections.title: Replay Detection With a Counter
sections.content:
The default replay detection method, RDM 1, puts an increasing counter value in the Replay Detection field. The receiver associates a replay counter with each sender and rejects any message containing an authentication suboption whose counter value is less than or equal to the last valid value it saw. DHCP servers may identify relay agents by giaddr value or by other data in the message, such as data in other relay agent suboptions. Relay agents identify DHCP servers by source IP address. When the replay detection value and the checksum are both valid, the receiver updates the last valid counter it holds for that sender.

All implementations must support the default RDM. Receivers should perform the replay-detection check before testing the checksum, because the keyed hash calculation is likely to be much more expensive than the replay-detection value check. This places a burden on the receiver to keep run-time state, the most recent valid counter value, for each sender, but the number of members in a DHCP agent-server system is unlikely to be unmanageably large.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a counter that grows over time. A receiver remembers the highest counter it has accepted from each sender and drops any message whose counter is not higher. This check runs before the hash is verified, because comparing two numbers is much cheaper than computing a hash.

sections.title: The Relay Identifier Field
sections.content:
The relay agent information option permits a relay agent to add its option to relayed messages without setting the giaddr field. In that case the eventual receiver of the message needs a stable identifier, so it can associate per-sender state such as the Key ID and the replay-detection counter.

A relay agent that adds a relay agent information option and sets giaddr must not set the Relay ID field. A relay agent that does not set giaddr may be configured to place a value in the Relay ID field, either a fixed value or one generated from other data such as its MAC or IP addresses. If the relay generates the value, it should select a value it can regenerate reliably, for example across reboots.

Servers that process an Authentication suboption should use the giaddr value to identify the sender if that field is set, and may be configured to use some other data in the message. If giaddr is not set, the server should use the Relay ID field if it is nonzero. If neither is set, the server may be configured to use other data in the message, or it may increment an error counter.
sections.plainLanguage: When a relay leaves the gateway address field empty, it can put its own identifier in the Relay ID field so the server knows which relay sent the message. The server uses that identifier to find the right key and the right counter.

sections.title: Computing the Authentication Information
sections.content:
The sender and receiver compute a hash across a buffer containing all of the bytes in the DHCP message: the fixed DHCP message header, the DHCP options, and the relay agent suboptions. Three values are set to zero for the computation. The hops field must be zero because its value may change in transmission. The giaddr field must also be zero because it may be modified in networks where one relay agent adds the relay agent option but another relay agent sets giaddr. The authentication information field in the Authentication suboption is set to all zeros, because the relay agent option is itself included in the computation. The relay agent option length, the Authentication suboption length and the other Authentication suboption fields are all included.

All implementations must support Algorithm 1, the HMAC-SHA1 algorithm, which is the HMAC protocol using the SHA-1 hash function. It requires a shared secret key configured at the relay agent and at the DHCP server. A 32-bit Key Identifier is associated with each shared key, and it is carried in the first four bytes of the Authentication Information field. The HMAC-SHA1 computation generates a 20-byte hash value, placed in the Authentication Information field after the Key ID, and the suboption length is then 38. The Key ID exists only so that a sender and receiver can pick a shared secret when more than one secret is in use among a network's relays and servers. Its values are entirely a matter of local configuration and only have to be unique locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides compute the same hash over the whole message. Before hashing, they set the hop count and the gateway address to zero and blank the hash field itself, so that fields which can change in transit do not break the check. The hash is a keyed one-way function: the relay and the server share a secret key, and only they can produce the same value.

sections.title: Sending and Checking a Relayed Message
sections.content:
To send a message, the sender sets the giaddr and hops fields to all zeros, appends the relay agent information option to the client's packet including the Authentication suboption, selects an appropriate replay detection value, puts its identifier into the Relay ID field or leaves that field as all zeros, sets the suboption length, places the replay detection value into the suboption and sets the algorithm to the number it is using. When using HMAC-SHA1 it sets the Key ID field, and it sets the field that will hold the checksum to all zeros. It then computes the checksum across the entire DHCP message and places the result into the Authentication Information field. Finally it restores the hops and giaddr values and sends the message.

To receive a message, the receiver examines the giaddr value and determines whether the packet includes the relay agent information option, then uses its configuration to decide whether it should expect an Authentication suboption. It must support a configuration that drops incoming messages that do not contain a valid relay agent information option and Authentication suboption. If it cannot determine which algorithm, key and RDM to use, or does not support the values indicated in the message, it should drop the message. Because this can indicate a misconfiguration that denies service to clients, it may instead notify its administrators or log an error.

The receiver then looks at the RDM field. Receivers must discard messages containing RDM values they do not support, and should report that condition by incrementing an error counter or writing a log message. If the replay value is not valid the receiver must drop the message, and it must not yet update the last valid Replay Detection value for the sender, because that field cannot be trusted until the checksum has been tested. If it trusted the replay value without testing the checksum, a malicious host could send a replayed message with a very high Replay Detection value and trick the receiver into rejecting legitimate messages from the sender. Finally the receiver sets giaddr and hops to zero and the Authentication Information field to all zeros, computes a hash of the message with the algorithm and key associated with the sender, and compares the result with the value sent. If they do not match it must drop the message; otherwise it updates the stored counter and processes the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender builds the message with the fields that can change set to zero, computes the hash over the finished message, and then puts the real hop count and gateway address back before sending. The receiver checks the counter first and then recomputes the hash. It accepts the message only when both checks pass.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has allocated a new suboption code from the relay agent option suboption number space for the Authentication suboption. The RFC also introduces two new number spaces that IANA maintains, one for the Algorithm field and one for the Replay Detection Method field.

The Algorithm identifier is a one-byte value. Value 0 is reserved and value 1 is assigned to the HMAC-SHA1 keyed hash. The RDM identifier is a four-bit value. Value 0 is reserved and value 1 is assigned to the use of a monotonically increasing counter value. Additional values in both spaces are allocated and assigned through IETF consensus, as defined in RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for two new number lists. One names the hash algorithm, where 1 means HMAC-SHA1. The other names the replay detection method, where 1 means a counter that always grows. Zero is reserved in both lists so that later versions can use it.

sections.title: Cost, Reordering and Alternatives
sections.content:
This protocol imposes a new computational burden on relay agents and servers, because they must perform cryptographic hash calculations when they send and receive messages. The burden may add latency to DHCP message exchanges. Because relay agents are involved when clients reboot, periods of very high reboot activity result in the largest number of messages to process. During a cable MSO head-end reboot event, for example, the time required for all clients to be served may increase.

Because DHCP is a UDP protocol, messages between relays and servers may be delivered in an order different from the one in which they were generated. The replay-detection mechanism will cause receivers to drop packets that are delivered late, leading to client retries. The retry mechanisms that most clients implement should not cause an enormous issue, but it will cause senders to do computational work which is wasted if their messages are reordered.

The Authentication suboption contains a four-byte Key ID, following the example of the DHCP Authentication option. Other authentication protocols, such as DNS TSIG, use a key name, which is more flexible and potentially more readable than a key id. On the other hand, it is crucial to minimize the size expansion caused by the relay agent information option, and named keys would require more physical space and more complex suboption encoding and parsing. These considerations led to a fixed-length Key ID instead of a variable-length key name.

The DHCP Working Group developed two documents describing authentication of DHCP relay agent options: this one and a separate one on authenticating relay agent options with IPsec. The Authentication suboption can be used without pairwise keys between each relay and each DHCP server. Where IPsec is readily available and pairwise keys can be managed efficiently, IPsec may be appropriate. If IPsec is not available, or there are multiple relay agents for which multiple keys must be managed, the protocol described here may be appropriate. Because the relay agents and the DHCP server are all in the same administrative domain, local network administration can choose whichever mechanism is more appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The protection costs work on every message, and that cost is highest when many clients reboot at once. Because DHCP uses UDP, messages can arrive out of order, and a message that arrives late is treated as a replay and dropped, so the client tries again. The RFC also points to IPsec as a different way to solve the same problem.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Suboption code 8 in the relay agent information option.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Octets of the algorithm, the RDM and all following fields.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Algorithm used to generate the authentication information.

fields.name: MBZ
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; set to zero.

fields.name: RDM
fields.desc: Replay Detection Method: 1 is a monotonically increasing counter.

fields.name: Replay Detection
fields.desc: Counter value used to detect replayed messages.

fields.name: Relay Identifier
fields.desc: Identifier for relays that do not set the giaddr field.

fields.name: Key ID
fields.desc: Identifier of the shared key used for the hash.

fields.name: HMAC-SHA1
fields.desc: Keyed hash over the whole DHCP message.

messages.label: BROADCAST REQUEST
messages.note: The client asks for an address and configuration.

messages.label: REQUEST WITH AUTH SUBOPTION
messages.note: The relay adds its information option, a counter and a keyed hash.

messages.label: REPLY WITH AUTH SUBOPTION
messages.note: The server checks the counter and the hash, then signs its own reply.

messages.label: BROADCAST REPLY
messages.note: The relay checks the server's hash before forwarding the reply.
